strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: distilling high-resolution image datasets without unrolling student training. Combining representative feature targets with per-class BatchNorm statistics is a sensible design.

The reported results are strong at larger image budgets. At 50 images per class, Table 1 reports 59.4% on Tiny-ImageNet and 57.6% on ImageNet-1K, compared with CDA's 48.7% and 53.5%, respectively. Evaluation across three datasets, multiple budgets, and three runs provides meaningful empirical evidence.

Cross-architecture experiments demonstrate useful transfer within the ResNet family: ImageNet-1K data distilled using ResNet-18 achieves 62.2% with ResNet-101 at 50 images per class. The ablations, regularization study, and synthetic-image visualizations provide additional insight.

The overall pipeline is understandable, and the paper credits the underlying optimal-transport algorithms, datasets, and inversion methods. The appendices acknowledge relevant limitations, including dependence on a pretrained classifier and propagation of source-dataset biases.
weaknesses: Baseline comparability is unresolved. At 10 images per class on ImageNet-1K, Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, whereas Table 3's baseline configuration reports 36.1%. Against WMDD's 38.2%, this changes the apparent improvement from 16.9 to 2.1 percentage points. The manuscript does not explain this discrepancy or establish that the headline comparisons use equivalent training and relabeling protocols.

The ablations provide limited support for attributing the gains primarily to Wasserstein matching. In Table 3, per-class BatchNorm with cross-entropy already achieves 64.0%, 41.3%, and 37.4%, compared with the full method's 64.8%, 41.8%, and 38.2%. These results demonstrate the importance of per-class statistics; stronger controls, particularly at larger image budgets, are needed to establish the central metric-specific contribution.

The mathematical contribution needs clearer positioning. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized support weights, Eq. (7) reduces to ordinary feature-space k-means quantization: each real feature can assign its mass to its nearest support point. This connection is neither discussed nor evaluated through a k-means prototype-inversion baseline using the same teacher and BatchNorm regularization. Consequently, the benefit of the proposed transport machinery over this simpler formulation remains unclear.

The MMD comparison does not isolate the claimed geometric advantage. At one image per class, the optimal squared-Wasserstein support point is exactly the class feature mean, making its feature-matching objective equivalent to linear-kernel mean matching when the encoder and regularization are identical. Table 4's 5.77% versus 0.48% therefore requires an explanation of those settings; removing augmentation and FKD alone does not establish a controlled metric comparison.

There are inconsistencies between the optimized distribution and the delivered dataset. Algorithm 2 learns nonuniform masses, but Algorithm 1 and Eq. (16) retain only support locations, without specifying corresponding weighting during student training or BatchNorm matching. The optimized and final empirical measures can therefore differ. Additionally, the fixed-transport quadratic Hessian does not establish convexity of the full support-optimization objective, and the updates divide by weights that the simplex projection permits to become zero.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. Table 6 measures only ImageNette at one image per class, where the barycenter reduces to a mean, and does not establish transport overhead at ImageNet scale with larger support sizes. End-to-end accounting of teacher training, feature extraction, and relabeling is unclear. The PDF also leaves important barycenter-solver settings, including initialization and step-size scheduling, unspecified.
